posts.title: Daniel Spates: A Schoolteacher, Two Mug Shots, and a $25 Reward
posts.description: Leavenworth portrait: D. D. Spates, prisoner no. 3399, in the front-and-profile photographs preserved with his 1903 federal prison record. In one photograph, D. D. Spates wears a dark jacket and a broad-brimmed hat. A small tag bearing the number 3399 is fastened near his collar. In another, attached to a Texas reward notice, he faces the camera bareheaded, dressed in a light-colored jacket. Beneath that second pair of portraits is the price offered for his capture: twenty-five dollars. Identified in my Ancestry research as Daniel Spates, he was born about 1877 in Wallis, Austin County, Texas. His parents were Howell Spates and Margaret Johnson. The family tree places his father’s death before 1880, when Daniel was still a small child.[4] Between these photographs lies a fragmentary story of a Black schoolteacher and minister, a federal prison sentence, a murder conviction, a reprieve from execution, and an escape. posts.title: Where is Lizzie Borden’s Mugshot?
posts.description: Portrait of Lizzie Borden in 1890, Wikipedia One of America’s most notorious nineteenth century murder defendants apparently escaped a routine indignity of criminal identification: the police mugshot. Was it because she was a respectable woman, or simply because police procedures had not yet caught up with the technology? On August 11, 1892, Lizzie Andrew Borden was arrested in Fall River, Massachusetts, and charged with the brutal murders of her father, Andrew Jackson Borden, and her stepmother, Abby. The murders had occurred one week earlier, on August 4, in the family’s home at 92 Second Street. Both victims had been attacked with a hatchet.[1] The case became a national sensation. Newspapers published portraits of Lizzie, illustrations of the murder scene, and detailed accounts of her appearance and behavior. Yet, curiously, there is no known police mugshot of the woman who would become one of the most famous murder defendants in American history. Why not? Mugshots Were Nothing New

posts.title: Elizabeth Dillon: The Pickpocket Who Wept at Funerals
posts.description: Elizabeth Dillon, photographed by police in March 1879, with her veil raised to clearly show her face. The portrait was first published in Thomas Byrnes’s Professional Criminals of America (1886). Elizabeth Dillon understood the value of a convincing appearance. In her later years, newspapers described a woman with a motherly smile, gentle manners, and a bonnet tied beneath her chin. She looked like someone a fellow shopper might trust. According to the police, that impression helped her steal.[1] Shops and crowded transit stations offered opportunities, but Dillon became particularly notorious for picking pockets in churches and at funerals. There, a display of grief could discourage suspicion. One newspaper account attributed this explanation to her: “No one suspects a person who cries well of being a thief.”[2] By the time she appeared in Thomas Byrnes’s Professional Criminals of America in 1886, she was already an experienced offender.
